questions.title: File I/O practice 1
questions.prompt: Which stream type reads from a file?
choices: std::ifstream
std::ofstream
std::cout
std::string
questions.explanation: An ifstream is an input file stream, while an ofstream sends output into a file.

questions.title: File I/O practice 2
choices: The body runs only after a successful read
It reads the entire file at once
It sorts the lines
It keeps the stream open forever
questions.explanation: The returned stream state becomes false when reading fails, preventing the loop from processing invalid data.

questions.title: Trace File I/O
questions.prompt: What output does this code produce? Enter each line in order.
accepted: One output line for each line in courses.txt.
questions.explanation: The loop processes each line only after getline succeeds, so it does not repeat stale data after the final read. The resulting output is 'One output line for each line in courses.txt.'.

questions.title: File I/O practice 5
questions.prompt: Why is `while (std::getline(input, line))` preferred over looping on `!input.eof()`?
choices: getline's result is false as soon as a read fails, so the last line is not processed twice
getline reads the whole file at once, which is faster
eof() is not a real function on input streams
getline automatically skips blank lines
questions.explanation: `eof()` only becomes true *after* a read past the end has already failed, so an `eof()`-controlled loop runs one extra time with stale data. Testing `getline` directly stops the moment a read fails. It reads one line per call (not the whole file) and does not skip blank lines.

questions.title: File I/O concept check 1
questions.prompt: A C++ program opens `courses.txt` without a folder path. Which statement is true?
choices: A path such as `courses.txt` is resolved from the program's current working directory, which may differ from the source-code folder. Print or configure the working directory when a file exists but the program cannot find it.
Overwrite existing records when the task calls for appending.
Assume every file path starts in the source-code folder.
Read data before checking for an I/O failure.
questions.explanation: A path such as `courses.txt` is resolved from the program's current working directory, which may differ from the source-code folder. Print or configure the working directory when a file exists but the program cannot find it. This matters because file code must be clear about paths, encodings, exceptions, and whether a write replaces or appends.

questions.title: File I/O concept check 2
questions.prompt: Which choice describes a reliable File I/O practice?
choices: Ignore character encoding for shared text files.
Check that opening succeeded.
Leave closeable resources unmanaged.
Catch an IOException where no useful response is possible.
questions.explanation: Check that opening succeeded. This matters because file code must be clear about paths, encodings, exceptions, and whether a write replaces or appends.

questions.title: File I/O concept check 3
questions.prompt: Which File I/O code review note is accurate?
choices: Use one giant string for a large file.
Build paths with fragile string concatenation.
Process data only after a successful read.
Treat a missing file as an empty valid file every time.
questions.explanation: Process data only after a successful read. This matters because file code must be clear about paths, encodings, exceptions, and whether a write replaces or appends.

questions.title: File I/O concept check 4
questions.prompt: Which File I/O habit prevents a common mistake?
choices: Write output before validating the destination.
Ignore partial read or parse failures.
Use platform-specific separators in portable code.
Know the working directory for relative paths.
questions.explanation: Know the working directory for relative paths. This matters because file code must be clear about paths, encodings, exceptions, and whether a write replaces or appends.

questions.title: File I/O concept check 5
questions.prompt: Which File I/O advice is accurate?
choices: Let stream objects close files through their destructors.
Hide the original file error behind a vague message.
Read all lines when streaming would keep memory smaller.
Assume the default charset is always the intended one.
questions.explanation: Let stream objects close files through their destructors. This matters because file code must be clear about paths, encodings, exceptions, and whether a write replaces or appends.

questions.title: File I/O concept check 6
questions.prompt: Which statement is accurate about File I/O?
choices: Mix persistence code with unrelated calculations.
Read and write files through streams with clear failure checks.
Open the same file twice for conflicting operations.
Forget that write modes can replace existing data.
questions.explanation: Read and write files through streams with clear failure checks. This matters because file code must be clear about paths, encodings, exceptions, and whether a write replaces or appends.
